description: We aim to build an interactive Mars exploration map using NASA data to help astronauts plan safe routes and identify scientific sites. By combining terrain, imagery, and environmental data, we want to make mission planning clear and practical. We welcome curious teammates interested in space exploration, coding, data analysis, visualization, and interface design. Join us to turn Martian data into a useful exploration tool!
summary:
Terra Ares 21 is an interactive Mars exploration planner that combines data from several NASA missions into one layered map so a human explorer can plan a safe Marswalk. Users stack real NASA Mars Trek imagery and terrain layers (CTX,
THEMIS, Viking, MOLA) and overlay the real traverses of the Curiosity and
Perseverance rovers. 
They place science targets and hazard zones, and the app computes a hazard-avoiding route with distances, walk-back limits and a timed EVA
schedule. Optimisers choose the shortest order or the most science within an EVA
time budget. The app also computes Mars sol date, season, sunrise/sunset and sun elevation, so the EVA can be placed safely inside daylight, and it shows dust-season and radiation context. Everything is labelled as measured, computed, reference or illustrative, so nothing is invented. 
It matters because the first crews will need one trustworthy view that combines routes, destinations, conditions and science goals, so they can finish their mission quickly and safely.
details:
Users pick a site (Gale Crater or Jezero Crater) and see a live map of Mars with adjustable-opacity NASA layers. They drag the base and targets, draw hazard zones, and click NASA rover waypoints to reuse real ground truth locations. A planner finds hazard-aware routes. The app then builds a timed EVA schedule in local solar time and checks it against daylight, EVA budget, reserve and walk-back limits.

Key features :

1. Multi-mission layer stack: MRO CTX, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, Viking, MGS MOLA, plus Curiosity and Perseverance traverses.

2. Hazard-aware A* routing: High zones are keep-out, Medium zones cost four times as much; legs show detour percentage.

3. Two optimisers: shortest order, and maximum science within the usable EVA time.

4. Sun, season and daylight calculation using the NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm.

5. Planning flags for budget, walk-back, daylight and hazards.

6. Export of the full plan (JSON) and the route (GeoJSON), plus GeoJSON import.

Benefits and impact: Crews and mission designers get one view instead of many separate portals. It shortens planning time and makes trade-offs visible.

Tools used: React, Vite, Leaflet, Node.js, Express, JavaScript. NASA Mars Trek WMTS tiles and NASA/JPL MMGIS rover feeds are the data sources. The backend proxies and caches NASA feeds.

Creative Aspect: It treats Marswalk planning as sun-aware, science-weighted route planning over real multi-mission data. The app probes each NASA layer at runtime and shows LIVE, ASSUMED or UNAVAILABLE, rather than failing silently.

Factors we considered:

1. Honesty about data: there is no live Mars weather (InSight ended in 2022), so conditions are computed or dated references.

2. Targets and hazards are illustrative and user-defined, and the router has no slope or rock raster.

3. The CTX mosaic is uncontrolled, so layers may be offset from each other.

4. Speed, budget and reserve defaults are planning placeholders.

5. Next step: derive slope and rock cost layers from DEM and HiRISE data.
